about: The rule catalog: every check edakit runs (P parts, G graph, E simulation, S schematic, L board, F manufacturing files) and every design hint (H), each with its rule, why it exists, what to do and where the knowledge comes from. Check IDs are stable: a retired check keeps its entry and its number is not reused. Hints have no rule a program could decide; 'when' says for which parts of the graph they apply. `edakit rules` prints this file, `edakit hints` the hints of a project.

P-1.title: graph pins = parts database
P-1.rule: Every part with an LCSC number – or, bought elsewhere, with a manufacturer part number in part – has a parts entry, its pins (number and name) equal that entry, and no supply pin is marked nc. When edakit part import has cached the library's symbol of the number, the graph's pins equal that symbol as well (case and blanks ignored, as S-2).
P-1.why: Checks, simulation, schematic generation and the BOM all read the parts entry. A pin number shifted by one, a wrong LCSC number or a missing entry makes them reason about another part than the one that gets assembled. A supply pin left open leaves an IC unpowered or powered through its I/O pins.
P-1.fix: Create the entry with the part-search skill; edakit part import <LCSC> reads pin numbers and names from the library symbol of exactly this part. Copy them into the graph. Names deliberately different from the symbol: waive P-1 on the component with the reason.
sources: edakit handbook 3.2 and 4.1

P-2.title: polarity sheet
P-2.rule: Every board gets a polarity sheet drawn from the Gerber data: each polarised part with copper, silkscreen, pad numbers, pin roles and nets.
P-2.why: Polarity at the footprint is what neither the graph nor the DRC can see: a library footprint once printed '+' next to the cathode pad. The sheet is what the second datasheet check (M-1) compares with the datasheet drawings, and what is compared with JLCPCB's assembly preview (M-2).
P-2.fix: Read the sheet against the datasheets. A wrong pad is fixed in the graph by swapping the nets and roles, not in the footprint.
sources: edakit handbook 4.4 and 8.1

P-3.title: own part = its source
P-3.rule: A board copied from another edakit project (own.what pcb, edakit part own) is that project's current datasheet and was copied from a commit, every datasheet a project writes (hardware/datasheet/) is of its current state, and a board that is not released at the state of its datasheet is a warning.
P-3.why: An own board has no distributor and no manufacturer's datasheet: its parts entry is derived from the project that designed it – pins, supply range, current, compliance. When that project changes, the copy describes another board than the one that gets plugged in, and every check of the host reasons about the old one. A copy of uncommitted changes names no state anyone can find again. A board that has not passed its own gate is not checked as a product, whatever its datasheet says – that is the user's decision, so it is a warning to accept, not an error.
P-3.fix: In the board's project: edakit part datasheet, then commit. In the host: edakit part own <path to the board's project>. Release the board there (edakit gate) and copy again, or accept the warning in the sign-off file with the reason.
sources: edakit handbook 4.5

P-4.title: parts orderable
P-4.rule: Every assembled part (an LCSC number, not bom: false) is in the stock snapshot of edakit stock, listed in JLCPCB's assembly catalogue, in stock for [project] quantity boards – under Standard PCBA with the assembler's attrition, max(placements + lossNumber, leastPatchNumber) – named as its parts entry names it, and not 'Standard Only' on an Economic order. MSL 5 or more (baked), stock below the need plus [project] stock_margin_pct and another library class than the entry's jlc_class are warnings; a part the snapshot lacks or could not read and a snapshot older than [project] stock_max_age_days are pending.
P-4.why: What the assembler can place is decided when the part is chosen, not when the BOM is uploaded. A part only LCSC stocks is 'pre-order only' at JLCPCB; a 'Standard Only' part (large holders, modules) turns a one-sided Economic order into Standard with setup per side and loading fees on every type; an MSL 5 part is baked for a fee and two days; a catalogue entry under another part number is another part. Found in the quote, each of these costs a part swap, sign-offs again and gate runs.
P-4.fix: edakit stock after every part change. A part that fails: another part (part-search, edakit stock --lcsc for the candidates), the part soldered by hand (bom: false), or Standard PCBA chosen on purpose ([release] assembly.pcba = "standard"). A wrong MPN: correct the parts entry or the LCSC number. Accept a warning in the sign-off file with its reason.
sources: edakit handbook 4.2 and 8.4
JLCPCB part pages (PCBA Type, MSL, X-ray) and the quotes of 2026-10-24 and 2026-10-25 (attrition)

P-5.title: supplier per part
P-5.rule: Every part bought separately and fitted by hand (bom: false) has an LCSC number or an order entry in its parts entry ({supplier: code} or {supplier: {code, moq, step}}), so that edakit order can put it into a cart. A warning.
P-5.why: The assembler's BOM leaves out every hand-soldered part, module and cable. What has no supplier and no order code is written into an order list by hand, late and without spares or the supplier's minimum – a 50-pack that does not exist, one LED short for the last board.
P-5.fix: Add order to the parts entry, e.g. {"berrybase": "OSM5DK7331A"} or {"lcsc": {"moq": 20, "step": 20}}, or give the component its LCSC number; then edakit order. Accept the warning in the sign-off file if the part is at hand already.
sources: edakit handbook 4.1 and 8.4

P-6.title: graph and parts entry name the same part
P-6.rule: Every component names the same part as its parts entry: the entry's lcsc equals its file name, the component's lcsc is no C99… user-library number (unless it stays out of the BOM, bom: false), its part names the entry's mpn (remarks in parentheses or after a semicolon left out, case ignored; a part that starts with a value, such as "330 Ω 0805", is that value), its value reads as the entry's value_ohm, value_f or value_h within 1 %, and its type fits the entry's kind (microcontroller and regulator: ic or module; transistor: npn, pnp, nmos, pmos; led: led or led_rgb; switch: switch or dip_switch; audio: buzzer; any other type the same word). A designator prefix that contradicts the kind (R, C, L, D, Q, U, J, SW, F, BT, BZ, K, TP) is a warning.
P-6.why: P-1 compares only pins, and every two-pin part has the same pins whatever it is. A number that points to another part, or an entry written for another number, passes stages P, G and E – and JLCPCB assembles what the number says, on every board. In the reference project the design document's LCSC numbers were wrong in eight places, found by hand against LCSC: C25789 ('74HC165') is a 464 kΩ resistor, C124327 ('10 kΩ') a crystal, six more did not exist. A C99… number looks like any other in EasyEDA's library, with supplier LCSC and class Extended Part, but nobody sells it.
P-6.fix: Correct whichever side names the wrong part: take the number by exact match from the catalogue (handbook 4.2) and write the entry from that number (edakit part import), or correct the graph's part, value or type. Replace a C99… number with an orderable part, or keep the part out of the BOM (bom: false) when it is plugged in or bought elsewhere. An intended mismatch – a part soldered by hand that borrows the entry of a sister part – is waived on the component with its reason.
sources: edakit handbook 3.1 (component fields type, lcsc, part, value), 4.1 (entry fields, kind, value parameters) and 4.2 (exact match only, C99… user libraries)
reference project: decision E-15, invalid LCSC numbers checked against LCSC on 2026-10-19 (C25789, C124327, C299999, C17236, C15942, C124278, C124279, C17347) and replaced

P-7.title: through-hole leads known and fitting the footprint
P-7.rule: Every part whose footprint has plated holes has lead data in its parts entry (field lead), and every hole of the footprint geometry – the board's pcb dump, else the library footprint of edakit part import – takes its lead at nominal size (L-9's test); less than 0.05 mm play in the worst case, or a plated slot narrower than 0.5 mm, is a warning. Without geometry it is not run.
P-7.why: L-9 finds a hole that does not take its lead only in the gate, on the drill file of a board that has been placed and routed: in the reference project every misfit was found there, five rounds over three days, each voiding the layout sign-off – the star LED's library footprint drilled 0.70 mm for 0.5 mm square legs (diagonal 0.71 mm), a USB-C receptacle's shell-leg slots failed after the board was reported done. The holes and the leads are known as soon as the part is chosen.
P-7.fix: Lead data from the datasheet into the parts entry (handbook 4.1); a footprint with larger holes, a part with thinner leads, or a decision (D-...) if the fit is accepted. L-9 checks the drill file again in the gate.
sources: JLCPCB PCB capabilities: hole size tolerance +0.13/-0.08 mm, minimum plated slot width 0.5 mm on 2 layers – https://jlcpcb.com/capabilities/pcb-capabilities (read 2026-10-27)
edakit handbook 13.6 and 8.1 (L-9)

G-1.title: structure
G-1.rule: Designators and net names are unique, every pin is in exactly one net or in nc, every net has at least two pins and a voltage range v, every part is on a known board, a net spans boards only through a cable, the layout requirements and the check settings name parts and pins of the graph, the ground net is a net of the graph, and purpose.use is private, gift or sale.
G-1.why: Everything after the graph is generated from it. A pin that is neither connected nor declared open is usually forgotten; a net with one pin is a typo or an unfinished connection; a net without a voltage range cannot be compared with pin limits and the simulation; a layout requirement or a check setting for a part that is not there protects nothing.
G-1.fix: Connect the pin, add it to nc when it is meant to stay open, correct the pin reference, give the net its range [min, max] over all operating states, or correct the names in layout, checks or ground.
sources: edakit handbook 3.1 and 3.2

G-2.title: pin locks
G-2.rule: Pins the firmware relies on are on the nets that checks.pin_locks of the graph names, and a pin table in the documentation equals the graph.
G-2.why: Firmware and hardware change in different files, often in different sessions. A GPIO that moved compiles fine and fails on the board.
G-2.fix: Change the graph, the firmware's pin table and pin_locks in one commit. Regenerate generated tables instead of editing them.
sources: edakit handbook 3.3

G-3.title: voltage domains
G-3.rule: The voltage range of every net stays within the vmax of every pin on it, and no active pin sees less than -0.3 V.
G-3.why: An input tolerates a few hundred millivolts beyond its supply; above that its protection diodes conduct, the pin is damaged or powers the IC through its input. A 5 V signal on a 3.3 V GPIO is the classic case.
G-3.fix: Level shifting (a divider, a series resistor with a clamp, a level shifter, an open-drain stage pulled up to the lower supply) or a part that tolerates the voltage; then correct v.
sources: the datasheet of each part: absolute maximum ratings, entered as vmax per pin

G-4.title: no floating input
G-4.rule: Every input has a driver or a pull resistor; an input that only MCU pins drive has a pull resistor; every bipolar transistor has a base-emitter resistor and every MOSFET a gate resistor to its source or to a rail.
G-4.why: A floating CMOS input takes its level from leakage and coupling: it reads random values and can rest in the threshold region where both input transistors conduct. An MCU pin is an input until the firmware configures it, so an enable or output-enable line it drives floats from power-up to that moment. A transistor whose base or gate floats can switch its load on during that time, or half-conduct and heat up.
G-4.fix: A pull resistor to the inactive level (10–100 kΩ); a base-emitter resistor or a gate-source resistor (10–100 kΩ) next to the transistor. If the floating state is harmless, waive it with the reason, for example data lines of a driver whose output enable is held off.
sources: TI SCBA004E, Implications of Slow or Floating CMOS Inputs (2021), section 1 – https://www.ti.com/lit/an/scba004e/scba004e.pdf

TI SLUA618A, Fundamentals of MOSFET and IGBT Gate Driver Circuits (2018), 3.5 dv/dt protection: a gate-source resistor holds the MOSFET off during power-up – https://www.ti.com/lit/ml/slua618a/slua618a.pdf

G-5.title: one driver per net
G-5.rule: At most one push-pull output or supply output drives a net.
G-5.why: Two outputs that disagree short the supply through their output stages: high current, heat, an undefined level.
G-5.fix: Separate the nets, make one side an input, or use open-drain outputs with a pull-up.
sources: edakit handbook 3.3

G-6.title: decoupling
G-6.rule: Every net with IC supply pins (power_in) has at least one capacitor to ground per supply pin.
G-6.why: An IC draws its current in short pulses. The inductance of the supply track turns each pulse into a voltage dip at the pin; a capacitor next to the pin supplies the pulse locally.
G-6.fix: 100 nF ceramic per supply pin next to the pin (the hand-over keeps it there on the board, L-12), plus the bulk capacitance the datasheet asks for.
sources: Analog Devices MT-101, Decoupling Techniques (Rev. 0, 2009) – https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-101.pdf

G-7.title: polarity
G-7.retired: Polarity is checked by the simulation (E-3: a reversed LED is reported as reversed or stays dark; E-4: every LED has a state E-3 checks) and, at the footprint, by the polarity sheet (P-2) and the second datasheet check M-1.
G-7.rule: Retired; the number is not reused.
G-7.why: A graph rule cannot see polarity; the simulation and the polarity sheet can.
sources: edakit handbook 3.3

G-8.title: voltage ratings
G-8.rule: Capacitors, diodes, transistors, MOSFETs, fuses, switches and connectors are rated above the largest voltage they can see; capacitors, diode VRRM and transistor VCEO, VDS and VGS with the factor 1.5.
G-8.why: Ceramic capacitors lose capacitance and lifetime near their rated voltage, semiconductors break down at theirs, and the declared ranges contain no spikes. The margin covers what a DC view does not see.
G-8.fix: A part with a higher rating, or a correct net range v if it is too pessimistic.
sources: edakit handbook 3.3 (the margins of the reference project)

G-9.title: parts signed
G-9.rule: Every part is verified against its datasheet (field verified), and no component has an open 'verify' note.
G-9.why: The parts database feeds every check. A value copied from a distributor's table without a look at the datasheet is an assumption; the sign-off records who checked what against which revision.
G-9.fix: Check the part (handbook 4.3) and fill in verified; resolve verify notes in the graph.
sources: edakit handbook 4.3

G-10.title: reverse polarity
G-10.rule: What a reversed source (battery holders, connectors in checks.reverse_protect of the graph) reaches through fuses, switches and connectors is only capacitors, the anode of a blocking diode or the drain of a PMOS whose source and gate are outside.
G-10.why: A battery inserted the wrong way or a reversed plug drives the supply negative; every IC on that rail conducts through its substrate diodes and dies within milliseconds.
G-10.fix: A Schottky diode in series (simple, loses 0.3–0.5 V) or a PMOS in the supply path with its gate to ground (milliohms; block reverse-pmos).
sources: TI SLVA139, Reverse Current/Battery Protection Circuits (2003) – https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slva139/slva139.pdf

G-11.title: I2C pull-ups
G-11.rule: Every I2C line (SDA, SCL) has a pull-up to a supply whose resulting value lies between (V - 0.4 V) / 3 mA and 10 kΩ.
G-11.why: I2C outputs are open-drain: they only pull low. Without a pull-up the line never goes high. A weak pull-up makes the rising edge too slow (rise time at most 1000 ns in Standard mode and 300 ns in Fast mode; Rp(max) = tr / (0.8473 × Cb)); a strong one cannot be pulled below 0.4 V by a device that sinks 3 mA.
G-11.fix: One pair of pull-ups per bus to the bus supply: 4.7 kΩ for 100 kHz, 2.2 kΩ for 400 kHz (block i2c-pullups). Modules often bring their own (pull in the parts entry) and parallel pull-ups add up. A pin called SDA or SCL that is not I2C gets another role in its parts entry.
sources: NXP UM10204 Rev. 7.0, I2C-bus specification and user manual (2021), 7.1 Pull-up resistor sizing and table 10 – https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/user-guide/UM10204.pdf

G-12.title: strapping pins
G-12.rule: A pin that an IC samples at reset (strap in its parts entry) is at its boot level through the circuit or its internal pull, and nothing on its net forces another level at power-up.
G-12.why: Many MCUs read boot options from pins at reset: the ESP32 starts its download mode when GPIO0 is low and sets its flash supply to 1.8 V when MTDI (GPIO12) is high. A pull resistor, a ground connection or another IC's output on such a pin keeps the board from booting - and only at power-up, so it is found late.
G-12.fix: Keep pulls and outputs that disagree with the boot level off strapping pins, or move the function to another pin. A button to ground on GPIO0 is fine: it is open at reset.
sources: Espressif ESP32 Series Datasheet v5.3, 3 Boot Configurations, table 3-1 – https://documentation.espressif.com/esp32_datasheet_en.pdf

G-13.title: flyback diode
G-13.rule: An inductive load on the board (relay coil, magnetic buzzer) that a transistor or an IC output switches has a diode across it, cathode at its positive terminal.
G-13.why: The current in a coil cannot stop at once. When the switch opens, the coil drives the switch's voltage far above the supply until something breaks down - 1000 to 1500 V for a 12 V relay without suppression. The diode lets the current circulate and clamps the spike to one diode drop.
G-13.fix: A diode directly across the coil: 1N4148 class for small coils, a Schottky such as SS14 for more current. For relays whose release time matters, a diode in series with a zener.
sources: TE Connectivity, The Application of Relay Coil Suppression with DC Relays (white paper) – https://www.te.com/en/products/relays-and-contactors/relays/intersection/relay-coil-suppression-dc-relays.html

G-14.title: USB-C sink termination
G-14.rule: A USB-C receptacle used as a power sink without a USB-C controller has its own 5.1 kΩ (±10 %) resistor from CC1 to ground and from CC2 to ground. A receptacle on a module or breakout states its termination in the parts entry (params.usb_c.cc: rd_5k1, controller or none); with none its CC pins need the two resistors, and without CC pins in the graph it fails.
G-14.why: A USB-C source switches VBUS on only when it sees the sink's pull-down Rd on a CC line. Without it a charger with a C-to-C cable delivers nothing, while C-to-A cables still work and hide the fault. With CC1 and CC2 on one resistor, an electronically marked cable adds its Ra in parallel and the source sees an audio accessory instead of a sink. A bought board brings its receptacle along – an MCU module with USB-C, a USB-C breakout – and such boards are sold with and without the two resistors; their CC lines are often no pins of the graph at all.
G-14.fix: Two resistors, one per CC pin, 5.1 kΩ to ground (block usb-c-sink). With a Type-C or PD controller on the CC lines this check stays silent. A module or breakout gets params.usb_c {"cc": "rd_5k1" | "controller" | "none", "source": "…"} from its schematic: with none, the two resistors on its CC pins (on the host board or soldered onto the breakout), or a board that has them; a receptacle never used with a USB-C source gets waive {"G-14": reason} on the part.
sources: Richtek AN064, USB Type-C/PD Brief Introduction and Analysis (2021): a sink asserts Rd on the CC pins – https://www.richtek.com/~/media/AN%20PDF/AN064_EN.pdf
USB Type-C Cable and Connector Specification (USB-IF): sink termination Rd = 5.1 kΩ

Waveshare RP2350-Zero schematic (RP2350_Zero.pdf, read 2026-10-27): R1 5.1 kΩ from CC1 (A5) and R3 5.1 kΩ from CC2 (B5) to GND on the module – https://files.waveshare.com/wiki/RP2350-Zero/RP2350_Zero.pdf

Lesson of the reference project (pytree E-18, 2026-10-25): the bought USB-C breakout Soldered 333011 has CC1 and CC2 on solder eyes and no resistors; found after the order list was written, by no check – the breakout was not in the graph

G-15.title: pin functions
G-15.rule: A net that states the function it needs (fn: pwm, adc, spi.sck|tx|rx|cs, i2c.sda|scl, uart.tx|rx) is on a pin whose parts entry lists that function; the nets of one fn_bus use one peripheral instance of the part; two PWM nets on one slice have the same fixed pwm_hz and never the same channel.
G-15.why: On most MCUs a peripheral reaches only some pins, and pins share hardware. On the RP2040 and RP2350 two neighbouring GPIOs share one PWM slice and with it counter, wrap and clock divider - one frequency for both; GP0 and GP16 even share the channel. An SPI data line on the clock pin, an analog input on a pin without ADC, a buzzer next to an LED dimmed at 1 kHz: each is a wiring fault that firmware cannot repair, and it shows only when that firmware is written.
G-15.fix: Move the net to a pin that has the function (functions in the MCU's parts entry), or give the PWM nets on a shared slice one frequency. A deliberate exception - bit-banged SPI, PIO - leaves fn out or gets waive {"G-15": reason} on the net. A pin without functions in its parts entry is not checked (a note): fill them from the pin-mux table of the datasheet.
sources: pico-sdk 2.1.1, src/rp2350/hardware_regs/include/hardware/regs/io_bank0.h: IO_BANK0_GPIOn_CTRL_FUNCSEL_VALUE_* – the SPI, UART, I2C and PWM function of every GPIO – https://github.com/raspberrypi/pico-sdk/blob/2.1.1/src/rp2350/hardware_regs/include/hardware/regs/io_bank0.h

pico-sdk 2.1.1, src/rp2_common/hardware_pwm/include/hardware/pwm.h: each slice drives two outputs from one counter; PWM_GPIO_SLICE_NUM = (gpio >> 1) & 7 below GPIO 32, channel = gpio & 1; src/rp2350/hardware_regs/include/hardware/platform_defs.h: RP2350A ADC_BASE_PIN 26

Lesson of the reference project (pytree D-14, 2026-10-19): the star's blue LED at 1 kHz and the buzzer on GP20/GP21 shared PWM slice 2 – every note would have changed the blue PWM; found by chance in a review

G-16.title: ground and supply pins
G-16.rule: Every pin of type ground is on the ground net or on a net joined to it (0 Ω bridges, inductors, or a net in the graph's grounds), and every power_in pin is on a net that a supply reaches – a power_output pin or a power input (battery holder, connector with a vbus pin or in checks.reverse_protect, simulation source) – directly or through fuses, switches, connectors, inductors, MOSFETs, resistors up to 100 Ω and diodes in forward direction.
G-16.why: P-1 makes the pin names equal the parts entry and G-1 connects every pin, but neither asks whether a pin is on the right net. A rail split by a typo in a net name, a ground pin on a net of its own, VDD swapped with a signal: each one kills every board and passes the other checks – G-6 counts capacitors per supply pin, so a split rail that took its capacitor along passes it too. The simulation shows such a fault only as a symptom, or not at all when the net's range is loose.
G-16.fix: Put the pin on its rail or on ground; it is usually a typo in a net name or two pins swapped. A ground that is separate on purpose (an analog ground joined at one point, an isolated side) goes into the graph's grounds. A supply pin fed from a GPIO or through a larger resistor gets waive {"G-16": reason} on its net.
sources: Lesson of the reference project (pytree MVP risk review, item 10, 2026-10-23): pin-to-net checked by hand for every IC, about 20 minutes, and nothing repeats it after the next change
edakit handbook 4.1 (pin types ground, power_in, power_output) and 3.3 (0 Ω bridges)

G-17.title: fuse against what it protects
G-17.rule: The hold current of every fuse – at the lowest ambient temperature (ambient_min_c in sim.json, from the fuse's i_hold_vs_temp) – is at most the i_max_a of every connector, switch and cable its current flows through; a trip current above that rating is a warning.
G-17.why: A polyfuse is chosen for the normal current. Below its hold current it never trips, and between hold and trip current its datasheet promises neither. A connector, switch or cable rated below the hold current carries an overload the fuse never stops: its contacts heat up instead of the fuse. The hold current rises in the cold – 1.5 A at 23 °C is 2.2 A at -40 °C. E-2 compares only the simulated operating currents with the ratings; the overload between the operating point and the trip current is in no scenario.
G-17.fix: A fuse with a lower hold (and trip) current, or a connector, switch or cable with a higher rating. A trip current above a rating accepted on purpose gets waive {"G-17": reason} on the fuse, e.g. 'normal current 0.9 A, a short trips within 100 ms'. Cables carry their rating as i_max_a in the graph's cables.
sources: PTTC SMD1206 HF Series, Rev. K (2017-01-03), p. 2: Ihold = maximum current the device passes without tripping, Itrip = minimum current at which it trips (23 °C still air); p. 4: thermal derating, SMD1206P150TFT 2.20 A at -40 °C, 1.50 A at 23 °C, 0.84 A at 85 °C – https://datasheet.lcsc.com/datasheet/pdf/c142bd6abe50067c0e2abbe967f2fcb5.pdf?productCode=C495353

Lesson of the reference project (pytree D-31/D-32, 2026-10-20): F1 (hold 1.5 A, trip 3.0 A) in series with two JST PH connectors rated 2 A – the trip current above the contacts, judged acceptable by argument only, recorded by no check

G-18.title: hot loop in the hand-over
G-18.rule: A part whose parts entry names its hot-loop pins (hot_loop: pin roles; a ground pin without a role is gnd) has a layout.loops entry on every net of that loop – the nets of those pins and, for a converter with a rectifier diode, the net behind the diode on its switch node (sw); a buck or boost IC whose entry has no hot_loop is a warning.
G-18.why: L-11 measures exactly the pad pairs that someone wrote into layout.loops or the board file's [[loops]], and H-5 counts as taken care of with any line in the graph's hints. The router connects by total length, not by current path, so a switching regulator whose loop nobody listed passes the DRC, every check and the gate however long its loop is routed. The segment that is routed far away is often not on a pin of the regulator: in a boost converter it lies behind the diode, between its cathode and the output capacitor.
G-18.fix: Write the loop into layout.loops of the graph – pad pairs of one net with max_mm and what, e.g. {"a": "D33.1", "b": "C13.1", "max_mm": 5, "what": "boost output loop"} – and L-11 measures it on the routed board. The parts entry gets hot_loop from the datasheet's layout section: a buck ["vin", "sw", "gnd"], an asynchronous boost ["sw", "gnd"]. A return that closes over the ground plane (L-11 measures tracks only) gets waive {"G-18": reason} on the ground net; a regulator whose loop is not on this board (a module) waive {"G-18": reason} on the part.
sources: TI SNVA021C, AN-1149 Layout Guidelines for Switching Power Supplies, Rev. C (2013), 5 Traces and Ground Plane: inductor, output capacitors and output diode as close to each other as possible; the grounds of IC, input capacitors, output capacitors and output diode connected close together directly to a ground plane – https://www.ti.com/lit/an/snva021c/snva021c.pdf

E-1.title: operating point
E-1.rule: The DC operating point of every scenario converges, and the simulation config fits the graph.
E-1.why: A scenario that does not converge checks nothing. Usually a node has no DC path to ground, a parameter is missing, or the config names a net or part that does not exist.
E-1.fix: Read the message: give a floating node a path (often a real design fault), complete the parts entry, or correct sim.json.
sources: edakit handbook 5.1

E-2.title: part stress
E-2.rule: Every part stays within its ratings with derating in every scenario: resistor power ≤ 50 %, currents ≤ 80 %, capacitor, diode and transistor voltages ≤ 67 %, LED forward current and reverse voltage, fuse hold current at the ambient temperature, contact currents, and the current of every MCU output pin and of all of them together. Every part whose entry gives rth_ja_k_per_w stays at ambient_c + P × Rth(j-a) ≤ its tj_max_c (at most the criteria's tj_max_c; LDOs and LED drivers in their E-3 item), and on a board of touch_c (sim.json, {board: °C}) at or below that touch limit.
E-2.why: A part at its absolute maximum rating is at the edge of failure, and worst-case supply, tolerances and ambient temperature only push it further. Derating buys lifetime and covers what a DC analysis does not see. An MCU's pins share one supply: each pin may be fine and the sum still beyond the package limit. Half the power rating is not a temperature: an AO3401A (125 K/W) at 0.45 W runs at 96 °C at 40 °C ambient, a diode's current and reverse voltage say nothing about its heat, and a part far inside its junction limit can still burn a hand – a P-MOSFET whose body diode feeds a rail from fresh cells, on the open underside of a board people pick up.
E-2.fix: A part with a higher rating, another value or another operating point; LEDs at MCU pins through a driver or a transistor. The derating factors in sim.json are a project decision. Too hot: lower the dissipation (a second MOSFET back to back, a lower RDS(on) or forward voltage, a larger resistor package), choose a package with a lower Rth(j-a), or move the part out of reach or cover it. touch_c comes from the standard the product follows, for the surface and the contact time people have with it – IEC 62368-1 TS1: 48 °C touched longer than a minute, 60 °C plastic (51 °C metal) for 10 s to 1 min, 77 °C (60 °C) for 1–10 s. The junction temperature is the upper bound of the surface; an entry without rth_ja_k_per_w and a board without touch_c get no item.
sources: edakit handbook 5.3

E-3.title: function
E-3.rule: The circuit does what it should in every scenario: supply currents within their limits, no supply fed backwards (into a source of sources at most its i_back_max_a, into each cell of a battery holder at most the i_charge_max_a of its cell state, both blocking_max_a – 1 mA – unless set), regulator outputs in tolerance, MCU supply and input levels defined, every part with an operating supply range (ratings vdd_op_min/vdd_op_max, or v_op on a pin) supplied inside it, measured to its own ground pin, every input with thresholds (vih_v|vih_ratio, vil_v|vil_ratio on the pin or in the params, a ratio of the part's supply) at ≤ VIL or ≥ VIH and the high level of every MCU output on its net reaching that VIH, MCU outputs on pins that can drive, driver headroom, LEDs on or dark as the load says, blocking diodes block, every net inside its declared range.
E-3.why: A circuit can stay within every rating and still not work: a regulator without headroom at the low end of the USB voltage, a 3.3 V signal into a 5 V input, a 5 V-only shift register or LED driver behind a 3.3 V MCU or an IC on a rail below its minimum behind a diode (within every absolute maximum, so G-3 sees nothing), an output assigned to an input-only pin, a reversed LED, a power bank that switches off below its minimum load, two supplies that meet where nothing blocks the way – the higher one feeds the lower one: into a PC's USB port through a module whose 5 V pin is its VBUS, into primary cells, which gas hydrogen when charged.
E-3.fix: Depends on the item; the protocol gives the actual and the expected value per scenario. A part outside its operating range or an input between its thresholds: supply the part from a rail inside its range, choose a part whose range and thresholds fit the rail and the driver (the TLC5916, 3–5.5 V with VIH 0.7 × VDD, for a TPIC6B595 behind a 3.3 V MCU), or put a level shifter between the domains; then correct the net's v. The range and the thresholds come from the datasheet's recommended operating conditions – a part entry without them gets no item. A supply fed backwards: block the path – a Schottky diode in the weaker supply's path, an ideal-diode or load-switch IC, two P-MOSFETs back to back – or exclude the combination by procedure and keep its scenario as info; a rechargeable cell charged on purpose gets the i_charge_max_a of its charger design.

E-4.title: LED has a known driver
E-4.rule: In every scenario every LED – each colour of an RGB LED – has a state E-3 checks: its cathode is on the output of a constant-current sink (directly, behind 0 Ω bridges or behind one balancing resistor), or the scenario's load has leds_on (listed: on, not listed: dark); an LED with neither, or one the netlist left out because its parts entry lacks a role the simulation reads, fails.
E-4.why: The simulation is the polarity check of the graph – G-7 is retired for it: a reversed LED is reported as reversed or stays dark where it should light. That holds only for an LED with an expected state. Without one E-3 skips it, and so does the netlist with an LED whose parts entry has no role anode or cathode (or those of its colour); its polarity and its current go unchecked and the run passes without a word.
E-4.fix: Give every load leds_on: the LEDs that light in it (the designator, or D10_RED for one colour of an RGB LED), [] when none does. Or put the LED's cathode on a driver output. An LED left out needs the roles anode and cathode – anode_<color> and cathode, or anode and cathode_<color>, for an RGB LED – in its parts entry (handbook 4.1).
sources: edakit handbook 5.3: a reversed LED elsewhere stays dark where it should light – the polarity check of the graph

S-2.title: schematic = graph
S-2.rule: Every schematic in EasyEDA has exactly the graph's parts (LCSC number, designator) and nets (pins, no-connects).
S-2.why: The schematic is generated, but EasyEDA can lose or move things: a generated schematic once drifted (a pin on two nets) without anyone writing to it.
S-2.fix: Generate it again (edakit schematic create, layout); never edit a schematic by hand.
sources: edakit handbook 6 and 13.2

L-1.title: PCB = graph
L-1.rule: The PCB has exactly the graph's parts, every pad carries the graph's net, and every graph pin has a pad.
L-1.why: Bringing parts into the PCB can lose, double or mismatch them, and a pad on the wrong net is routed wrong without any DRC error.
L-1.fix: edakit pcb parts --write and edakit pcb nets --write.
sources: edakit handbook 7 and 8.1

L-2.title: copper from the Gerber files
L-2.rule: The copper rasterised from the exported Gerber files connects every net, shorts no two nets and contains every connected pad.
L-2.why: This is what the factory gets. Pours, islands and export settings can differ from what the editor shows, so the last connectivity check does not trust EasyEDA.
L-2.fix: Look at the routing picture, route again or refill the pours, then export again.
sources: edakit handbook 8.1

L-3.title: DRC
L-3.rule: EasyEDA's design rule check reports nothing after save and reload.
L-3.why: Clearances, widths and open connections below the manufacturer's limits. Right after API changes the DRC reports false errors, so it runs after a reload.
L-3.fix: edakit route reload, then fix what remains (route all, the plan).
sources: edakit handbook 7 and 9

L-4.title: footprint = parts database
L-4.rule: Every part in the PCB has the footprint named in its parts entry.
L-4.why: A swapped footprint variant (another pitch or package) fits in the editor and not on the board.
L-4.fix: Correct the parts entry, or swap the part with edakit pcb parts --write.
sources: edakit handbook 4.1

L-5.title: track width
L-5.rule: Every track is at least as wide as IPC-2221 asks for 1.5 × the largest simulated current (failure) and as the practical width of its net class (warning); the voltage drop is shown as an upper bound.
L-5.why: A track too narrow for its current heats up and drops voltage; the class width adds robustness for manufacturing and for later changes.
L-5.fix: Wider tracks or a pour for the net; net classes in [routing.classes] and [net_classes] of the board file.
sources: IPC-2221B, Generic Standard on Printed Board Design: conductor width for a current
edakit handbook 5.4

L-7.title: placement plan
L-7.rule: Fixed parts sit where the plan says (±0.02 mm, rotation, side), and the plan itself has no findings: outline, overlaps, holes, through-hole pins under parts on the other side, near distances.
L-7.why: The auto-layout or a move by hand can shift a connector, a button or an LED that the enclosure or the user relies on.
L-7.fix: edakit pcb apply; correct the plan in the board file.
sources: edakit handbook 7

L-8.title: polarity marks
L-8.rule: Every '+' or '-' in the silkscreen – a PCB text, or a '+' a footprint draws as two crossing strokes of 0.3–2 mm in the silk Gerber file – sits next to a pad of that sign: the nearest pad on its side whose pin role has a sign (anode…, plus…, vbus '+'; cathode…, minus… '-') has the same one.
L-8.why: A sign at the wrong pole makes whoever solders or inspects the board turn the part the wrong way. The sign that counts most is the footprint's own print: the assembler, the hand-solderer and JLCPCB's assembly preview go by it. In the reference project the library footprint of a 5-mm LED printed '+' at the pad that symbol and datasheet call the cathode. L-8 read only PCB texts, and a cathode had no sign, so a '+' at a cathode was compared with the anode next to it and passed; a review found it before five boards were assembled with the LED turned.
L-8.fix: Compare the footprint with the datasheet. The print is right: correct the roles in the parts entry. The datasheet is right: put the anode's net on the pad with the '+' and give that pin the role anode (handbook 4.4), or use another footprint. A cross inside the box of a [[silk.art]] item is artwork and is not read; a decorative cross elsewhere is waived on the nearest part (waive L-8).
sources: edakit handbook 4.4 and 8.1

L-9.title: hole fits the lead
L-9.rule: Every through hole takes its lead at nominal size (lead data in the parts entry); less than 0.05 mm play in the worst case, or a plated slot narrower than 0.5 mm, is a warning.
L-9.why: Nobody else checks library footprints: the Christmas bell's Nano footprint had 0.9 mm holes for 0.64 mm square header tails (diagonal 0.91 mm). JLCPCB drills plated holes +0.13/-0.08 mm.
L-9.fix: A footprint with larger holes, a part with thinner leads, or a decision (D-...) if the fit is accepted.
sources: JLCPCB PCB capabilities: hole tolerance and minimum plated slot – https://jlcpcb.com/capabilities/pcb-capabilities
edakit handbook 13.6

L-10.title: pads as in the library
L-10.rule: Every pad sits where the library footprint has the pad with that number; intended swaps are listed in pad_map.
L-10.why: A pad swap made in the PCB to fix a polarity can be reset by EasyEDA, and the board is then assembled with the original, wrong assignment.
L-10.fix: Fix polarity in the graph (handbook 4.4) instead of swapping pads; list intended swaps in pad_map.
sources: edakit handbook 4.4

L-11.title: short current loops
L-11.rule: Each pad pair listed in [[loops]] of the board file or in layout.loops of the graph is connected over tracks within its length limit.
L-11.why: A switching regulator's loop carries pulsed current; a long loop radiates and rings. In the reference project it was routed 61 mm across the board, and the layout review found it, not a check.
L-11.fix: Put the regulator, its capacitors, the diode and the inductor together and route the loop first.
sources: TI SNVA021C, AN-1149 Layout Guidelines for Switching Power Supplies (2013) – https://www.ti.com/lit/an/snva021c/snva021c.pdf
edakit handbook 8.2

L-12.title: layout requirements of the circuit
L-12.rule: The plan keeps what the circuit hands over: every part in layout.fixed, layout.edge and layout.near of the graph is fixed, an edge part sits within edge_mm of the outline, a near part within near_mm of its host, and every IC with a supply pin is fixed with a capacitor of its own from that supply to ground within near_mm.
L-12.why: The auto-layout knows nothing about belonging – it once put a decoupling capacitor 24 mm from its IC. And what the circuit designer knows about the board – which connector is plugged in from outside, which part a person presses or looks at – is lost when it lives only in a conversation: the PCB designer works in a session of its own and gets only what is written down.
L-12.fix: Fix the part in [place] of the board file where the requirement holds. A requirement that cannot be kept goes back to the circuit designer as a written request – the layout side does not change the graph. A derived decoupling that does not apply is waived on the IC with its reason (waive L-12).
sources: Analog Devices MT-101, Decoupling Techniques (Rev. 0, 2009) – https://www.analog.com/media/en/training-seminars/tutorials/MT-101.pdf
edakit handbook 7.4 and 14.1

L-13.title: pads of different parts keep the clearance
L-13.rule: Every pad keeps at least the routing clearance (clearance_mil) from every pad of another part on another net, on each copper layer both are on; a pad without a net counts as a net of its own. route check measures it before anything is written to EasyEDA, stage L on the pads of route read while they are the PCB's.
L-13.why: Freerouting cannot move a pad, route check measured tracks and vias only, and the plan (L-7) compares part boxes, not pads. In the reference project two resistors of the star stage stood with their pads 0.09 mm apart: they passed both and were routed, and a layout review found them, not a program. EasyEDA's DRC (L-3) sees it only after the copper is written, with EasyEDA's own rule. JLCPCB makes SMD pads of different nets 0.15 mm apart at the least; the default clearance of 6.5 mil (0.165 mm) is above that.
L-13.fix: Move or turn one of the two parts in [place] of the board file (fix it there if the auto-layout put it) until the gap is at least the clearance, then place and read the board again. Pads of one part belong to its footprint and are not checked. A pair that is close on purpose is waived on one of its parts or nets with the reason (waive L-13).
sources: JLCPCB PCB Manufacturing Capabilities, minimum clearances: SMD pad to pad clearance (different nets) 0.15 mm (read 2026-10-26) – https://jlcpcb.com/capabilities/pcb-capabilities

JLCPCB, Terms and Conditions of JLCPCB Assembly Service (updated 2026-09-09), 2.2: placement and gap of the components after IPC-7351B medium or low density, components with very small gap avoided – https://jlcpcb.com/help/article/61-Terms-and-Conditions-of-JLCPCB-Assembly-Service
edakit handbook 7.5 and 8.1

L-14.title: SMD pads of different parts leave a paste gap
L-14.rule: On every side that is assembled ([release] assembly sides), every SMD pad keeps at least the paste gap ([release] assembly paste_gap_mm, 0.4 mm) from every SMD pad of another part on another net; a pad without a net counts as a net of its own. route check measures it before anything is written to EasyEDA, stage L on the pads of route read while they are the PCB's.
L-14.why: The copper rules let pads of neighbouring parts come as close as the clearance (L-13), but both pads get paste, and where only a thin web of the stencil separates the prints the paste can bridge in reflow. That short appears only at assembly, and the bare-board test cannot find it. JLCPCB adjusts the stencil apertures itself and names no minimum web, so the project's paste layer does not settle it; its assembly terms ask for placement and gaps after IPC-7351B medium or low density and rule out high density. At the nominal level each courtyard reaches about 0.25 mm beyond the largest pad, so two parts whose courtyards just touch keep their pads about 0.5 mm apart; 0.4 mm stays below that. In the reference project the paste of a ground pad and a transistor base pad of neighbouring parts was 0.06 mm apart and passed every check; the layout review found it.
L-14.fix: Spread or turn the two parts in [place] of the board file (fix it there if the auto-layout put it) until their pads are at least the paste gap apart, then place and read the board again. Pads on one net (a capacitor at its own supply pin) and pads of one part are not compared, nor through-hole pads or pads on a side that is not assembled. A pair that is close on purpose is waived on one of its parts or nets with the reason (waive L-14).
sources: JLCPCB, Terms and Conditions of JLCPCB Assembly Service (updated 2026-09-09), 2.1 and 2.2: footprints, placement and gap of the components after IPC-7351B medium or low density, high density not supported, components with very small gap avoided – https://jlcpcb.com/help/article/61-Terms-and-Conditions-of-JLCPCB-Assembly-Service

L-15.title: copper per side: no bare area, no loose copper
L-15.rule: Per copper layer the Gerber copper's share of the board area and its largest copper-free circle inside the pour outline are reported; on a layer the board file pours, a copper-free circle above [copper] max_bare_mm (5 mm) is a warning, a share below [copper] min_cover on any layer is one, and on every layer so is a copper piece that touches no pad, via or plated hole (copper inside an NPTH or mounting hole is drilled away).
L-15.why: EasyEDA drops every pour piece that touches no pad of its net, so where the pour net has no pad that side stays bare – and a pour that was never filled, or was filled before the last copper change, looks the same in the files. L-2 checks only connectivity, EasyEDA's DRC (L-3) does not report a missing fill, and route pours treats a read-back mismatch as harmless. In the reference project half the back of a released board stayed bare (47 % copper, a copper-free circle of Ø 9.7 mm) where its ground net had no pads; the gate and the layout review passed it, and it was seen by eye the evening before the order. Islands kept for stitching (route pours, stitch) stay on the board as loose copper when the second fill does not run.
L-15.fix: A bare area on a poured layer: give it to a net that reaches it – a second pour net on the layer (pour_regions, priority) or a pad or via of the pour net there – then route pours and run the gate again. Loose copper: connect it with a via or a track, or delete it, and fill the pours again without islands. An area bare on purpose (an antenna keep-out): accept the warning with its reason. [copper] max_bare_mm and min_cover = {TOP = %, BOTTOM = %} in the board file set the limits of a board.
sources: edakit handbook 7.6 (pours: EasyEDA drops islands, readback-mismatch) and 8.1 (L-2)

L-16.title: annular ring and hole-to-hole spacing
L-16.rule: Every plated hole keeps JLCPCB's annular ring on TOP and BOTTOM – a component hole 0.18 mm (2 layers, 1 oz; below 0.20 mm a warning), a via 0.05 mm (via Ø at least hole + 0.1 mm) – from the hole's edge to the nearest point without copper in the Gerber files; and every two plated holes, also two of one part, keep JLCPCB's hole-to-hole spacing edge to edge: 0.45 mm when a component hole is one of them, 0.2 mm between two vias.
L-16.why: Nothing else looks at the copper around a hole or at the web between two holes: L-9 compares a hole with its lead, L-13 the pads of different parts. A footprint whose holes are widened so that the leads fit, as L-9 asks, loses ring and web on the same pitch; the fab then grows the pads, asks back (an engineering query costs about a day across time zones) or plates a ring that breaks out. In the reference project a four-leg RGB LED at 1.25 mm pitch had its holes widened to 0.80 mm with pads of 1.06 mm: a ring of 0.13 mm, below the fab's absolute minimum, passed the gate and went into the order remark. Via pairs 0.47–0.50 mm apart were flagged by a review against a figure from memory and put on the order checklist; the fab's table allows 0.2 mm.
L-16.fix: Grow the pad or shrink the hole, as far as L-9's lead fit allows. Where the pitch allows neither, a footprint whose pitch carries hole + 2 × ring + the pad clearance, or a part with a matching hole pattern. Holes too close: move a via or a part, or take a smaller hole where L-9 still passes. A part whose ring the fab confirmed is waived in the graph with the reason (waive L-16 on the part or its net).

L-17.title: silkscreen as printed
L-17.rule: On each side, edakit's own print – the designators, texts and artwork of silk apply, i.e. what is not in the print silk apply found before placing anything – lies on no solder-mask opening. Warnings: other print on an opening (per part, the part of the nearest pad), print beyond the board outline (per side), a part of the designators side with no visible designator, no group label and no line in [silk] unlabelled (per part), and a text height edakit prints below 1.0 mm (per value).
L-17.why: Every reroute moves vias and parts, so a designator that had room loses it; silk apply only says 'without room' and goes on, its own check of the openings is a separate command, and print beyond the outline was checked nowhere. JLCPCB clips print on openings, prints nothing beyond the board edge, and calls characters below 1.0 mm unidentifiable. In the reference project a test point never got a label and three designators were lost after reroutes, each found on pictures or in a review; the released tree board passed the gate with footprint print on the mask openings of 11 parts and 3.3 mm² of print beyond its outline.
L-17.fix: Own print on an opening: run edakit silk apply again after the last routing. Footprint print on an opening or beyond the outline: correct the footprint, or accept the warning. A part without a designator: give it room, a group label ([silk] groups), or list it in [silk] unlabelled with the reason. A text below 1.0 mm: raise label_h_mm, board_label_h_mm or h_mm, or accept the warning.

F-1.title: BOM = graph
F-1.rule: The BOM generated from the graph equals EasyEDA's BOM per designator, and every LCSC number is in the parts database; parts with bom: false are left out on purpose.
F-1.why: JLCPCB assembles what the BOM says; a part that EasyEDA lists differently from the graph ends up differently on the board.
F-1.fix: Correct the graph and bring the PCB in line (edakit pcb parts --write).
sources: edakit handbook 8.1

F-2.title: stock at JLCPCB
F-2.rule: Every BOM line is in JLCPCB's assembly catalogue with stock for [project] quantity boards, under the MPN of its parts entry (case and blanks ignored); another library class than the entry's jlc_class is a warning.
F-2.why: LCSC's stock and JLCPCB's assembly stock differ. A part that is not available can only be pre-ordered, which delays the order or changes the price.
F-2.fix: A part in stock (part-search skill); a cheaper part that is available is worth a gate run.
sources: edakit handbook 4.2

F-3.title: pick and place
F-3.rule: Every BOM part is in the pick-and-place file exactly once with the PCB's side and rotation, and only on the sides [release] assembly allows (Economic PCBA: one side, SMD only).
F-3.why: A missing or doubled line is a missing or doubled part; a part on the wrong side needs Standard PCBA at a higher price.
F-3.fix: Move parts to the allowed side in the plan, or mark hand-soldered parts bom: false.
sources: edakit handbook 8.4

F-4.title: files of one run
F-4.rule: Gerber ZIP, BOM and pick-and-place file come from the same gate run, with their SHA-256 in fab/manifest.json.
F-4.why: Files from different states fit together only on paper; the manifest is the record of what was ordered.
F-4.fix: Run the gate again and upload only from its folder.
sources: edakit handbook 8.3

F-5.title: Gerber set
F-5.rule: The Gerber set is complete; outline and mounting holes equal the plan (±0.2 mm); tooling holes are in the NPTH drill file with the mask open and no copper in the opening.
F-5.why: A missing layer or a shifted outline is found at the factory at best; tooling holes with copper or mask make JLCPCB add their own.
F-5.fix: Export again; correct outline, holes or tooling holes in the board file and apply them.
sources: edakit handbook 7 and 8.1

F-6.title: order settings = board
F-6.rule: With [order] in the board file: the remark has at most 200 characters, all ASCII; mark = "specify" has the placeholder JLCJLCJLCJLC on a silkscreen layer, at least 0.8 mm high in [[silk.texts]] (a height not given there is a warning); a placeholder with another mark is a warning; an Economic order with fewer than 2 tooling holes is a warning; no copper of either side lies within tab_copper_mm (1.0 mm) of a declared tab zone of the outline, measured on the Gerber files. The outline stretches free of copper are listed, and fab/<board>/order.md holds the form.
F-6.why: The order form fields that depend on the board are filled in by hand while ordering: a cart with 'Remove Mark' prints the placeholder as text, a remark of 202 characters does not fit the field, a remark that allows tabs where a track runs 0.45 mm from the edge lets the tab cut it, and an Economic order without own tooling holes gets JLCPCB's, possibly on a visible edge. Each was found late in the reference project, the tooling holes only in the quote.
F-6.fix: Correct [order] of the board file – a shorter ASCII remark, mark = "specify" with the placeholder (or another mark), tab zones only on stretches order.md lists as free, or the copper moved back from the edge – or add [tooling] holes. A warning the owner wants (JLCPCB's tooling holes, a hand-placed placeholder) is accepted in the sign-off file.
sources: edakit handbook 8.4

H-1.title: bulk capacitor at the power input
H-1.why: A supply cable has inductance. With only ceramic capacitors at the input, plugging in rings, and the voltage can overshoot to about twice the supply. Load steps (a servo starting, LEDs switching) also need charge close to the input.
H-1.fix: An electrolytic or polymer capacitor of 10–100 µF near the input connector - its series resistance damps the ringing - rated at least 1.5 × the input voltage (G-8).
sources: Linear Technology AN88, Ceramic Input Capacitors Can Cause Overvoltage Transients (2001) – https://www.analog.com/media/en/technical-documentation/application-notes/an88f.pdf

H-2.title: MOSFET gate resistor
H-2.why: The gate capacitance and the inductance of the drive loop form a resonant circuit; a fast edge makes it ring, which can exceed VGS max and radiate. A GPIO that switches a small MOSFET slowly rarely needs anything.
H-2.fix: 10–100 Ω in series with the gate, close to the gate, when the driver is fast or far from the gate; keep the gate-source resistor (G-4).
sources: TI SLUA618A, Fundamentals of MOSFET and IGBT Gate Driver Circuits (2018), 2.8 Effects of parasitic components – https://www.ti.com/lit/ml/slua618a/slua618a.pdf

H-3.title: debounce buttons and switches
H-3.why: Mechanical contacts bounce: Ganssle measured about 1.6 ms on average and up to 6 ms, one switch 157 ms. A counter or an interrupt sees several presses.
H-3.fix: Debounce in firmware: sample every 5–10 ms and accept a level after it was stable several times. An RC filter with a Schmitt-trigger input only where firmware cannot, for example a wake-up from sleep.
sources: Jack Ganssle, A Guide to Debouncing – http://www.ganssle.com/debouncing.htm

H-4.title: inductive load off the board
H-4.why: A motor, solenoid or relay at the end of a cable stores energy in its coil like one on the board, but G-13 sees only coils that are parts of the graph. When the transistor switches off, the coil's voltage spike lands on it.
H-4.fix: If the load at this connector is inductive: a diode across the connector's load pins on the board, cathode at the supply pin; a Schottky for PWM.
sources: TE Connectivity, The Application of Relay Coil Suppression with DC Relays (white paper) – https://www.te.com/en/products/relays-and-contactors/relays/intersection/relay-coil-suppression-dc-relays.html

H-5.title: switching regulator layout
H-5.why: The loop of input capacitor, switch and diode or second switch carries pulsed current; its area radiates and its inductance rings. A ceramic input capacitor helps only next to the IC's VIN pin.
H-5.fix: Input capacitor next to the VIN and GND pins, the loop as small as possible, and the loop listed in layout.loops of the graph so that L-11 checks it.
sources: TI SNVA021C, AN-1149 Layout Guidelines for Switching Power Supplies (2013), 3 Filter capacitors – https://www.ti.com/lit/an/snva021c/snva021c.pdf

H-6.title: lithium cells need protection
H-6.why: Li-ion and LiPo cells must not be over-discharged (below about 2 V per cell), overcharged or short-circuited, and protection circuits are mandatory for Li-ion packs. Alkaline and NiMH cells tolerate all of this far better.
H-6.fix: For lithium cells: protected cells or a protection IC between holder and circuit; a cut-off in the firmware is not enough while the MCU is off. For alkaline or NiMH cells nothing is needed.
sources: Battery University BU-304, Why are Protection Circuits Needed? – https://batteryuniversity.com/article/bu-304-why-are-protection-circuits-needed
Battery University BU-304a, Safety Concerns with Li-ion – https://batteryuniversity.com/article/bu-304a-safety-concerns-with-li-ion

H-7.title: ESD at external connectors
H-7.why: A connector that a person touches or plugs a cable into sees electrostatic discharges of several kilovolts. A line that runs straight to an IC pin relies on the IC's internal protection.
H-7.fix: For lines that leave the enclosure: an ESD diode (TVS) per line, as near to the connector as the design rules allow; a series resistor on slow signal lines.
sources: TI SLVA680A, ESD Protection Layout Guide (2022) – https://www.ti.com/lit/an/slva680/slva680.pdf

H-8.title: two supplies on one net
H-8.why: Where two supplies meet on one net, the higher one feeds the other whenever its path has nothing that blocks: primary cells get charged, a PC's USB port takes current, a body diode conducts and heats. A single P-MOSFET switched off by the other supply is no block – its body diode conducts from drain to source. G-10 looks at a reversed source only, and the simulation shows the back-feed only in a scenario with both supplies on and the other one higher. Whether it matters – cells that may be charged, a host that tolerates it, an operating rule – is a judgement.
H-8.fix: A blocking element in every path that must not be fed: a Schottky diode (0.3–0.5 V drop), two P-MOSFETs back-to-back with a common source (block power-or-pmos), or an ORing controller. Or an operating rule that firmware or manual enforce (one of the two unplugged). The hint names the net and marks the supplies that reach it without a block; record how it is handled: "hints": {"H-8": "Q8/Q9 back-to-back, D40"}.
sources: AOS AO3401A, Rev 3.1 (December 2023), p. 2: body diode forward voltage VSD -0.7 V typ., -1 V max. at IS = -1 A and VGS = 0 V, body-diode continuous current IS -2 A – the diode conducts with the MOSFET off – https://datasheet.lcsc.com/datasheet/pdf/fee353dd1e9e0bc90b295f14f381aa4c.pdf?productCode=C15127

Lesson of the reference project (pytree D-44, 2026-10-23): with one AO3401A cutting three AA cells off while USB-C was plugged, fresh lithium cells (5.4 V) fed through its body diode, about 0.7 W and up to 125 °C on a touchable underside; a second AO3401A back-to-back fixed it

Lesson of the reference project (pytree D-47, USB tree, 2026-10-25): the module's 5V pin is its USB VBUS without a diode and J1 feeds the same rail through D32 – a source at J1 above the PC's VBUS feeds the PC through the module (about 0.2 A at 5.25 V against 4.75 V, second check M-1); accepted with an operating rule

H-9.title: read-back of a serial output
H-9.why: Shift registers and constant-current LED drivers shift on the rising clock edge and change their serial output a propagation delay after it – the STP08CP05 typically 21–24 ns and at most 32 ns at 3.3 V, the TLC5916 12–30 ns at 3 V. SPI mode 0 samples on that same rising edge: a read-back in mode 0 works only while the delay is longer than the MCU's input hold time, and only the datasheet's minimum delay counts – the STP08CP05 states none. Mode 1 samples on the falling edge, but shifts the MCU's own data out on the rising edge, where the part samples its serial input. The SPI mode is the firmware's, so no program decides this from the graph, and the question gets lost between the concept and the code.
H-9.fix: Look up the output's delay after the clock edge (out_edge and t_pd_ns on the pin of the parts entry) and the MCU's SPI input hold time in the mode the firmware uses. If the minimum delay is not safely longer: read back by bit-bang, sampling after the falling edge, or test the SPI read on the first board with bit-bang as the planned fallback. Record the decision in the graph: "hints": {"H-9": "…"}.
sources: ST DocID13524 Rev 8 (STP08CP05, August 2018), table 8 Switching characteristics: CLK-SDO tPLH 21/28 ns (typ/max) at VDD 3.3 V and 17/22 ns at 5 V, tPHL 24/32 ns at 3.3 V and 19/25 ns at 5 V, no minimum; table 9 and figure 8: data shifts and SDO changes on the rising CLK edge

TI SLVS695D (TLC591x, June 2007, revised January 2015), pin functions: CLK "Clock input for data shift on rising edge"; 7.7 Switching Characteristics (VDD 3 V): tPLH4 and tPHL4 CLK to SDO 12/20/30 ns (min/typ/max)

Wikipedia, Serial Peripheral Interface, section Mode numbers (read 2026-10-26): mode 0 (CPOL 0, CPHA 0) shifts data out on the falling SCLK and samples on the rising SCLK; mode 1 shifts on the rising and samples on the falling SCLK
